rv.q: In a season of overhyped shows, the evident sincerity, the effort, the fervent belief in character – and Warren’s occasional transcendence – feels refreshing.
Here, Warren’s performance is the only thing to truly soar.
Jonas, simply, cannot. Or does not.
But in a musical, if you’re not pulling for said relationship to survive and if you don’t believe you are watching a real partnership that could live or die before your eyes, nothing works.
Sung by Jonas, it’s basically incomprehensible — to be fair, that’s at least in part because of the generally murky sound.
Brown’s show deserves better than the serial missteps of this 85-minute faux pas de deux.

Now, add in woefully miscast leads in Nick Jonas and Adrienne Warren and barely-there direction by Whitney White and what you get is the dirge that opened Sunday night at the Hudson Theatre — one of the worst musical productions of the season.
Her bravura performance pointedly demonstrates that she can singlehandedly carry a show on her own

Warren is a marvel, her powerful voice and expert skills as an actress painting a complete portrait of the defiantly happy, defiantly determined and defiantly angry Cathy. She’s properly mournful in the melancholy “Still Hurting”; hilarious in the vaudevillian “A Summer in Ohio”; and cockeyedly opti...
Their performances never quite come together, and the material demands more compatibility than this production delivers.

But that happens here, so the songs became more about the actors than the characters, and the emotional connection dries up — just like tear ducts.
Jonas and Warren try as hard as they can to animate Jamie and Cathy, but they are more plausible as solo, self-explaining units than as a two-person relationship in formation and freefall.
All the same, White has crafted an intriguing and intellectually ambitious revival, one that embraces the brutal emotional honesty of Brown’s source material.
Director Whitney White and a skillful design team honor the piece’s two-planks-and-a-passion minimalist roots, while offering plenty to delight the eye and ear.
Jonas, though, seems to be the wrong actor in the wrong show.
For The Last Five Years to succeed, both players must deliver equally vibrant turns.
There’s no emotional payoff in these two stories traveling in opposite directions.
But for this relationship to matter to us, we have to discern something – anything — that drew them together in the first place.
Unfortunately, this long-awaited debut is a frustrating misfire — overproduced, emotionally hollow, and fundamentally at odds with the delicate intimacy that makes the musical so beloved.
The score—stunning in its complexity and melodic heft—is emotionally transportive.
What does make this production worthwhile are the lush orchestrations that weave emotions into each musical number.
It’s a treat to have The Last Five Years on Broadway after all these years, but it’s hard to escape the feeling that the show could do better than this.

cn.t: Brown's beloved song cycle falters in its long-awaited Broadway debut, with critics citing uneven casting (Jonas struggles, Warren shines) and an overproduced staging that undermines the show's intimate essence.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.
